newsitem.title: JAPAN: Moderate demand for Italy Euroyen bond-underwriter.
newsitem.headline: Moderate demand for Italy Euroyen bond-underwriter.

text.p: Italy's 100 billion yen 20-year Euroyen bond issue has attracted moderate demand since its launch on Tuesday, but demand from Japanese investors weakened from the previous issue in October, underwriters said on Wednesday.
"Demand has not been as strong as last time, but that doesn't mean that this issue is a failure as the issue has already generated moderate interest," an underwriter said.

Underwriters said the issue was primarily absorbed by smaller institutional investors, including regional investors, credit associations and credit unions, as demand from major investors such as life insurance firms has been lacklustre.

"We're not planning to buy the Italian issue at this point. The spread has narrowed and the coupon is not attractive enough to draw strong interest from major life insurers," a senior manager at a major Japanese life insurance firm said.
The Euroyen bonds, which were lead-managed by Nikko Europe, are due March 2017 and carry a coupon of 3.45 percent, the lowest ever obtained by Italy in the Euroyen market.
The spread over the equivalent 20-year Japanese government bond was 16.4 basis points.
Italy has offered 20-year bonds three times before.
In October, Italy offered 100 billion yen worth of 3.7 percent 20-year bonds with a spread of 22 basis points.
For the current issue, however, smaller investors' demand was still strong due to the scarcity of similar Euroyen bonds.
The Italian issue was still more attractive than Japanese corporate straight bonds with similar maturities.
"There are very few comparable long-term bonds in the Euroyen market so the Italian issue should draw the interest of many investors," a second underwriter said.
"The Euroyen bonds are still more competitive than the recent 20-year corporate bonds issued by Japanese firms," the underwriter said.
"Although the issue is unlikely to be absorbed as quickly as the previous ones, I think the bonds will be sold out."
